title: PAUL THE PROPHET AND IDOL WORSHIP

sense.text:
“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments.” You gain a good understanding when you keep God’s commandments. Fearing God and keeping his laws is how you gain understanding of the text. That is the clear understanding of the Bible.

That is why so many cannot receive Paul. Israelites say Paul was a white man, a Roman, a heretic. Others are slicker: they throw out little messages, that Paul was only giving his opinion there, or that Paul was advocating idolatry, so the people come to the conclusion on their own that Paul is wicked. The problem is that Paul is in the way: in the way of people doing what they want to do, in the way of men who want multiple women at one time and call them wives.

If you are not keeping God’s commandments and you are still doing worldly negro things, with one toe in the Bible and a whole foot in the world, you are not going to break down Paul’s letters.

“Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.” This is Stephen blasting and cursing out the wicked elders of the schools that came against him. As their fathers resisted the Holy Ghost, so did they.

“Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?” The prophets spoke about the Messiah, “the coming of the Just One”, and they were slain for it. The murderers of the prophets had children, and those Pharisees and Sadducees were those children: the descendants of the men who killed the prophets that foretold Christ are the ones who killed the Messiah himself, “the betrayers and murderers.” And the men Stephen said it to knew that their fathers were murderers of the prophets.

They “received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it”: they resisted it. Resisting the Holy Ghost goes back to the law. The Holy Spirit spoke through the prophets, they wrote it down, and that is the law itself.
“They were cut to the heart” because it was true: their fathers killed the prophets that spoke of Christ, and they killed Christ. “They gnashed on him with their teeth”: they cursed him out.

Being “full of the Holy Ghost”, Stephen saw “the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God.” He saw two separate entities, the Father and the Son: the Father sitting, and the Messiah standing up to welcome him home. He did not see the Son of man standing inside the Father, as if they were one entity, three in one. He saw him standing beside his Father.
They “stopped their ears”, cast him out of the city and stoned him, “and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man’s feet, whose name was Saul.” This is Saul, who became the apostle Paul.

“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit”: Christ was standing up to receive him. “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge”: forgive them. “He fell asleep”: he died. The Lord allowed him to see the Father and the Son because he was going to die anyway.

“And Saul was consenting unto his death”: Stephen’s death. At this time Saul was the enemy of the church; he agreed to Stephen’s stoning.

In that “great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem” they were killing anyone who followed Christ, and locking them up. They were scattered through Judea and Samaria, “except the apostles”: the apostles remained in Jerusalem, while the disciples of the disciples, like Philip and the deacons, scattered abroad. There had been seven deacons, and they had killed one of them.

Saul went “breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord”, and asked the high priest for letters to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any “of this way”, the teaching, men or women, “he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem”: locked up.

“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” “I am Jesus whom thou persecutest.” How was he persecuting Christ, when Christ was gone? When you persecute the disciples and the apostles, you persecute Christ, because he resided in them. Saul was not locking up or killing Christ himself; he was killing those Christ dwelled in.

“It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks”: hurting the Lord’s prophets, he was harming himself. A lot of Israelites are doing the same now, bringing harm on themselves by persecuting Christ through the spirit of Paul and the apostles.

“Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” What should I do then? The men with him stood “hearing a voice, but seeing no man”: they heard Christ speak but could not see where it was coming from. Saul “was three days without sight”, blinded by the glory of Christ, “and neither did eat nor drink”: he fasted.
Paul saw in a vision Ananias coming in and laying his hand on him, “that he might receive his sight.”

Ananias answered with what he had heard, “how much evil he hath done to thy saints at Jerusalem”, and that he had “authority from the chief priests to bind all that call on thy name.” This guy was killing us. He has the authority from the Pharisees to have us arrested and killed. You want me to heal him?

“Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me.” What is Paul? A chosen vessel unto Christ. Christ picked him: do what I tell you; I chose him; heal his eyes.

He was chosen “to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel”: the Gentiles are the northern kingdom first, then the heathen kings, and the children of Israel are the southern kingdom.
“For I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” Keep that in mind: great things Paul must suffer for Christ’s name’s sake.

Ananias was sent that Saul might receive his sight “and be filled with the Holy Ghost”, just like Stephen was. Not filled with the holy opinions, the holy mistakes or the holy errors: filled with the Holy Ghost.

Scales fell from his eyes, he “arose, and was baptized”, and “straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.” Saul, who was persecuting the church and killing its members, was visited by Christ himself, redeemed from that lifestyle and converted to Paul an apostle. His life was changed forever from that day forward.

“I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city”: a good place. And he spake to the people “in the Hebrew tongue.” Paul was a Jew of Cilicia. He was not a Roman or a white man.

“Brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel”: Paul came from a high, prestigious family, and he sat and learned under a famous teacher, Gamaliel, a Pharisee. He was “taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers”, a very prestigious background of schooling in the law, born and raised a Pharisee and “zealous toward God”. He was not an idiot who sat down and wrote errors and mistakes into his letters, like some of the idiots say on YouTube.

“I persecuted this way unto the death”: this doctrine, this teaching. He was killing people that followed Christ, “binding and delivering into prisons both men and women”, locking them up for following that way.

“After the most straitest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee”: the strictest sect. He was born and raised a Pharisee, under the feet of Gamaliel, and learned the perfect manner of the law. That is Paul’s background.

“The gospel which was preached of me is not after man”: not of man, not his feelings, his opinions or his emotions. That is what the Bible says. But Israelites, Christians and negroes in the world alike say otherwise. They can’t say it outwardly, because they would face backlash, so they throw out bits and pieces of doubt: Paul was saying some things that ain’t biblical, some things not really according to the law. The listener goes, well, if Paul made these mistakes he ain’t no apostle, he’s wicked, and they are held unaccountable: we didn’t say he’s wicked, that’s your conclusion.

That is contingency talk: throwing certain things out there to see if people are going to bite, so they can say at the same time, I didn’t really say he’s wicked. It is nothing new among us. With time, experience and elders you can decipher those things.
“Neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ”: Christ revealed himself to Paul and taught him.

In the Jews’ religion he was a Pharisee under Gamaliel. “Beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it”: he went all out, a head hunter, hunting us down like animals and killing us. He “profited in the Jews’ religion above many my equals” because he was a Hebrew of the Hebrews, from a family of status, “being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers.”

“Who separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace”: it was revealed to Paul that the Lord had already chosen him from the beginning, despite what he did. He was chosen to be a prophet, the same thing God said to Jeremiah.

“To reveal his Son in me”: the Father revealed his Son in Paul; the spirit of Christ was in Paul. “That I might preach him among the heathen”: among our people who are living as heathen.

“Immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood”, and he did not go up to the apostles at Jerusalem at first. He had been our enemy, so he couldn’t come to us right away. He went into Arabia and returned to Damascus.

“Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter”: he went to meet the elder. It took three years because he had been killing us wholesale; he had to prove himself before they could say, okay, we can trust this guy, he’s teaching the gospel, go see Peter. He “abode with him fifteen days”, two weeks and a day, learning from Peter. So Peter knew Paul pretty well.
Of the other apostles he saw none, “save James the Lord’s brother”: James who wrote the book of James, Christ’s brother.
“Behold, before God, I lie not”: I am not writing lies to you about what I saw.

He “was unknown by face unto the churches of Judea”: they didn’t know who he was. They had heard only that “he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed”: the one who was killing them had repented.
“And they glorified God in me”: they glorified Christ, the God in him.

precepts.why:
“Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee”: he knew Paul too, and that is what Paul just said. “Before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee”: I chose you. “And I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.”

Just as Jeremiah was sanctified before he came out of the womb, Paul was separated “from my mother’s womb” and called by God’s grace: chosen to be a prophet. It is the same exact thing, being said by Paul. The Lord chose him before he was formed, despite what he did before Christ met him.

“For I have appeared unto thee for this purpose”: the I is Christ, who appeared to Paul personally, “to make thee a minister and a witness”, a minister, an apostle, and a witness of the things he had seen and of the things in which Christ would yet appear unto him.

He was sent “to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light”: from sin to the laws of God and the faith of Christ, “and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.”

So Christ told Paul what his mission was: you’re my minister; you’re going to go out there and pull your people out of darkness into the light. He was sanctioned for that mission, and Christ taught him directly; then he went to Peter and sat at his feet and learned from him. That is the Son revealed in him.

Why go through all of this? Because Negroes are evil and they hate Paul’s letters, because Paul’s letters contest a lot of the things that Negroes in Israel and in the world like to do or want to do.

sense.text:
Fourteen years after, Paul went up to Jerusalem “by revelation” and communicated “that gospel which I preach among the Gentiles”: among the northern kingdom, Israel scattered among the Gentiles. That is the heathen he is referring to.

“But privately to them which were of reputation”: he taught those scattered among the Gentiles, but he also sat down personally with those he knew believed. “Lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain”: he would not teach the unworthy.

“Because of false brethren unawares brought in”: the Pharisees and them, who could not destroy the doctrine, were infiltrating it. Paul himself had been sent to kill those teaching Christ, so the teachings were held in schools in secret, and Paul had to teach privately those he knew were sincere. Their lives were in danger. The false brethren were spies, sent in to find out where the teaching of Christ was, so the believers could be locked up and killed.

You even have Israelites today who flex on YouTube that they have moles and spies in our congregation. It is only alleged, and not to be believed at all, but saying it alone says who you are. It is very odd that the very people who were killing the disciples back then sent forth spies, and now Israelites are bragging about sending forth spies. It sounds almost like what Stephen said: you are the children of the murderers that killed the prophets that taught Christ; you are those guys today.

They “came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage”: back under the old law of sacrifice.

“To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour”: Paul ignored them. He would not entertain those who did not believe in Christ, rebellious scoffers, not for an hour, “that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.”

“Whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me”: I don’t give a damn what their status was, who they thought they were, what their reputation was, who they believed themselves to be. You don’t believe in Christ, kick rocks, get out of here. Repent or die. That is how Paul was: he didn’t sit around arguing back and forth with you all day. Those who “seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me.” Paul is very blunt and clear.

“The gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me”: to teach the uncircumcised, the Gentiles of our people, the Gentile Israelites, “as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter”: to teach the Jews, born and raised in the law. “He that wrought effectually in Peter”, the same spirit, the Son, “was mighty in me toward the Gentiles”: toward the northern kingdom, the scattered Israelites.

“James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars”: Peter, James and John were the elders, the three main top men. They “perceived the grace that was given unto me”: they saw in the spirit that the Lord was dealing with Paul. They gave Paul and Barnabas “the right hands of fellowship”: they made them ministers, apostles, “that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.” Paul to the northern kingdom, the scattered Israelites; they to the Jews, the southern kingdom.

Remember Christ asked Saul why he persecuted him. Was Paul killing Christ and locking Christ up? No. He was killing and locking up the spirit of Christ in the people. That is what persecuting him meant.

“He that heareth you heareth me”: he that hears the apostles and the disciples hears Christ, because he resides in them. “He that despiseth you despiseth me”: so if you hate Paul, you hate Christ. If you hate Peter, James, John, Matthew, Mark, Luke or Timothy, you hate Christ. If you hate the prophets, you hate Christ.

“And he that despiseth me despiseth him that sent me”: despise Christ and you hate the Father too. It goes in that order, because Christ is our head and the Father is his head.

This is where all the confusion about Paul lies. “Now as touching things offered unto idols”: that is the context, things offered to idols. “We know that we all have knowledge”: concerning idols, they all knew they had knowledge. Keep that in mind; Paul goes on to explain what that knowledge is.

When you read Paul’s letters, the understanding comes either above the verse, within the verse or under the verse. If it is not found in those three places, he will often address the same situation in a different church, in a different letter, with more clarity, because the same situations tended to occur in multiple churches, and you cross reference them together.

“Knowledge puffeth up”: knowledge can puff you up and make you arrogant. “But charity edifieth”: whatever knowledge you may have, charity is the most important thing. Charity translates to love your neighbour as yourself. Charity is love.
“He knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know”: you know enough, but you don’t know everything. Don’t get arrogant. Don’t be puffed up.
“If any man love God, the same is known of him”: you will be known whether you love God by your actions.

“As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols”: the context has not changed from verse 1. Paul is addressing eating things offered to idols.

“We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one.” The root of the word knowledge is to know. The knowledge the believers in Christ had in verse 1 is this: idols are nothing in the world. Idols are not gods; there is no God but one. Be mindful of what you know, and don’t get an ego from what you learn.

Paul was born and raised in the perfect manner of the law; he was not a fool. When he wrote letters, his source material was the law and the prophets. So whatever he says in this letter, we can go back into the law and find it there.

“For though there be that are called gods”: Zeus is called a god. Odin, Thor and Loki are called gods. Vishnu, Krishna and Allah are called gods. White Jesus is called a god. Bacchus, Mars, Mercury, Ares, Ashtoreth and Baal are called gods. “Whether in heaven”: some are known to dwell in heaven, paradise, Nirvana or Olympus; “or in earth”: some on earth, or under the water like Poseidon.

“As there be gods many, and lords many”: the Hindus have 37,000 gods, and yoga calls upon those gods. Don’t do yoga. Its positions are bowing down to them, which the law says not to do.

“But to us there is but one God”: to us, the Israelites. We are monotheistic; the other nations are polytheistic and worship many gods. “The Father, of whom are all things”: he is the architect. “And one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him”: his Son, whom he used to make everything, the master builder. Christ made us, and the Son was made by the Father. Grandfather, father: not the same entity. My dad is not my grandfather; my dad’s dad is my grandfather.

“Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge”: the knowledge of verse 4, that idols are nothing in the world. “For some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol”: some, stronger in the faith, understood that idols are nothing; others ate meat offered to idols and really believed in their own mind they were honouring that god. “And their conscience being weak is defiled”: defiled in believing that these idols are actually real gods.

Some of our people scattered among the nations were former idolaters, and others were raised heavily in Judaism to abhor and abstain from all idols at any cost. That was the dilemma here.

“But meat commendeth us not to God”: to be commended is to gain acknowledgement, to be accepted, like being commendable for your service around the house or at your job. Paul explains it within the verse: “for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse.” Eating meat sacrificed to idols, or not eating it, does not bring you closer to God or further from him, because idols are nothing in the world.

If I set a Ninja Turtle toy by my plate and pray, oh heavenly Donatello, heavenly Leonardo, thank you for this chicken, does the food become defiled? No. I’m an idiot eating food. Heavenly Power Ranger, heavenly Zordon, heavenly Thundercats: the meat remains the meat. But some will say, you prayed to Ninja Turtles, that food is bad. That is the weak conscience. A lot of people really believe that doing that makes the food bad.

“But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.” The liberty is the knowledge that idols are nothing in the world, action figures. Be mindful, because not all your brothers are as strong as you. If I eat food offered to a toy action figure and a brother with a weak conscience, from an idolatrous background, sees me, he may think I’m an idolater, or that maybe it’s okay to worship the turtle. If that offends your brother, don’t eat it, because it will make him fall.

If you don’t know, you just don’t know: liberty means, once again, the knowledge that idols are nothing in the world. And you that know it are to be mindful of a brother or sister who is weak in the faith. Christians don’t understand that part, and it is the foolery they attack the prophets with today. Take good notes; if this is fluent to you, it will not be a problem.

“For if any man see thee which hast knowledge sit at meat in the idol’s temple”: in the Greco-Roman world Paul was writing to, in Corinth in Greece, temples were hubs for more than worship. Our own temple was multipurpose: sacrificing, feast days and worship, and business transactions too, until Christ got mad and threw the tables over. The heathen temples were also multipurpose: banquet halls, like the restaurants of today or the halls we rent for our feast days with a catering service, and community and business gathering spaces, rented out.

After an animal was sacrificed to an idol, a portion of the meat was burned, a portion given to the priest, and the rest eaten in a meal on the temple grounds or sold in the public market. It was the same with Levi in our temple: the meat was burned, eaten by the priests and by those who offered it, and the rest put in the storehouse. Some believers in Corinth with a strong conscience went to those meals and ate, knowing the idols were not real and the meat was just food. They went there for the food.

But the brother who comes from an idolatrous background sees you sitting there, and his conscience is “emboldened to eat those things which are offered to idols”: he is convinced it’s okay to worship and reverence idols. That was a real point of disagreement and a stumbling block for those with a weak conscience, who felt it was a compromise with idolatry. Paul is saying, I get it, you know the idols around here are nothing, but you are offending other believers who are weaker, and leading people to believe we partake in idolatry. If it is going to cause your brother to fall, don’t eat there.

“And through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?” You will either make him go back to idols or make him denounce the faith, because he sees you eating food offered to idols.

“But when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ”: you sin against Christ for being a bad example to your brother. As verse 1 said, knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. Look out for your brother.
“Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth”: if eating there makes my brother offend, I will not eat that food.

precepts.why:
“And there ye shall serve gods, the work of men’s hands, wood and stone”: there, in the lands where we are scattered, we would serve gods made by men, carved in wood and stone, or molten in silver and gold. Back then those were the idols of old; in modern times it would be Christianity and Islam. Make-believe gods, action figures called gods: Ken and Barbie called gods, Ninja Turtles, Transformers, Power Rangers called gods. Made by men’s hands, “which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell”, because they’re not alive. They’re toys. Nothing in the world.

The there is in verse 27: “And the Lord shall scatter you among the nations, and ye shall be left few in number among the heathen.” Who is Paul writing to in Corinthians? Israelites. Corinth is in Greece. Israel is scattered among all nations and all lands, Greece, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Iraq, Iran, India, Hawaii, Fiji, Madagascar, so Paul is writing to Israelites living in a foreign land. That is us being scattered, what Moses was talking about.

So when Paul says an idol is nothing in the world, he is saying what the law already said.

“And have cast their gods into the fire: for they were no gods.” How do you cast a god into a fire? Because there isn’t a god. They were nothing in the world, “but the work of men’s hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them.” They are destroyable because they are toys. Put a toy in the microwave on the highest heat and it’ll melt. It is not a god.

“He is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the Lord made the heavens.” All the gods of the nations are idols; our God made the heavens.

That is what Paul said: we know, we have the knowledge, that there is but one God, one true God, with the Son.

“Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands.” The nations’ idols are sculpted to have mouths, like an action figure has a mouth, “but they speak not”. Eyes they are given, “but they see not”: that is what Moses said. Ears, but they hear not; noses, but they smell not. Hands, “but they handle not”: they can’t hold anything. Feet, “but they walk not.”

“They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.” They that make them are just like them, dead objects, and so are you that believe these things are real gods: dead like your toy, dumb like your toy, fake like your toy. That is what David said.

David says it again: “The idols of the heathen are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they speak not; eyes have they, but they see not; They have ears, but they hear not; neither is there any breath in their mouths.” They’re not alive. “They that make them are like unto them: so is every one that trusteth in them.” David said it twice: nothing in the world.

See what David’s son says about idols. “But miserable are they, and in dead things is their hope, who called them gods, which are the works of men’s hands”: the nations. “Gold and silver, to shew art in”: the art is the eyes, the ears, the nose, the mouth, the colour, the paints. “And resemblances of beasts”: an idol made like an animal, like a goat.

“Or a stone good for nothing”: you kiss it and it does nothing for you. “The work of an ancient hand”: it has been around since ancient idolatry.

“But that which is made with hands is cursed, as well it, as he that made it”: the idol is cursed, and he that made it is cursed, “because he made it; and it, because, being corruptible, it was called god.” Corruptible because it can be destroyed: it grows old, it rusts, it rots, and it was called a god.

“For the ungodly and his ungodliness are both alike hateful unto God”, and “that which is made shall be punished together with him that made it”: not only is the idol destroyed, the person that made it is destroyed along with it.

“Therefore even upon the idols of the Gentiles shall there be a visitation”, because they are “stumblingblocks to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the unwise.” Esau is going to pay for that, and Ishmael is going to pay for Islam too.

“Both they that make them, they that desire them, and they that worship them, are lovers of evil things”: we saw that at the 2819 church. They “are worthy to have such things to trust upon”: they are evil as hell, and they are going to die.

The potter, “tempering soft earth”, fashions vessels “for our service”: he makes pots and bowls and sells them to the people. Some “serve for clean uses”, a bowl, a vase to hold flowers, and some do the contrary. But “employing his labours lewdly”, wickedly, “he maketh a vain god of the same clay”, the same soft clay used to make bowls and cups, “even he which a little before was made of earth himself.” A man making a god makes no sense. How can a man, a mortal being, make an eternal being? It’s ridiculous.

He returns to the earth “when his life which was lent him shall be demanded.” Your body doesn’t belong to you: your life was lent you. This is a rental, and the same way you got it, you have to return it. That means not getting high, not getting drunk, not defiling your body. It belongs to him, and it shall be demanded.

The idol maker “striveth to excel goldsmiths and silversmiths” and “counteth it his glory to make counterfeit things”: going out of his way to prove he is better than a goldsmith or a silversmith by making fake gods. “His heart is ashes, his hope is more vile than earth, and his life of less value than clay”: the lives of those who make idols are worthless, “Forasmuch as he knew not his Maker”. He doesn’t care about the God that made him; he cares about making gods.

“And all the enemies of thy people, that hold them in subjection, are most foolish”: the heathen that have us in captivity are stupid, “more miserable than very babes”, because they are not God’s people. They have no God, no guidance; they are not chosen at all. They are here to make our lives hell for breaking God’s laws; outside of that they have no purpose. By default, every nation outside of the nation of Israel, their god is the devil. Satan plays with your imagination, and the nations make gods according to their imagination: heathen gods are figments of heathen imagination. And Israelites have adopted those gods into our lives.

“For they counted all the idols of the heathen to be gods: which neither have the use of eyes to see, nor noses to draw breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers of hands to handle”: the same thing his father David said.

“For man made them, and he that borrowed his own spirit fashioned them”: your spirit was lent to you; it is a loan. “But no man can make a god like unto himself”: no man can make a god that can see, hear, eat, think and walk. So idols are nothing in the world.

An example of meat in the idol’s temple. “Now the Babylonians had an idol, called Bel”: as Paul said, there be that are called gods, gods many and lords many. Beelzebub means lord of the flies; Baal-peor; Bel means lord. It all goes back to lords: gods are lords.

“There were spent upon him every day twelve great measures of fine flour, and forty sheep, and six vessels of wine”, huge vessels, all to reverence this idol. “And the king worshipped it, and went daily to adore it: but Daniel worshipped his own god.”

Asked why he did not worship Bel, Daniel answered, “Because I may not worship idols made with hands, but the living God, who hath created the heaven and the earth, and hath sovereignty over all flesh.” That is what David said, what Moses said, and what Solomon said.

sense.text: “Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?” Paul is an apostle.

Paul reminds the Corinthians how “all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea”: their fathers, the Israelites, passed through the sea with Moses, “And did all eat the same spiritual meat”.

“With many of them God was not well pleased”, and “these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things”. Verse 7 is the context: “Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them”, back in the wilderness: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play”, into idolatry.
Now he gets to the point. “Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to wise men”: to men who have understanding. “Judge ye what I say”: listen, pay attention.

“The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” When we drink the wine and break the bread, it is for Christ’s sake. “For we being many are one bread, and one body”: we are all part of that body in Christ.

“Behold Israel after the flesh: are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?” Israelites born and raised in the law went and sacrificed in the temple, and they not only sacrificed the animals there, they partook of the sacrifices by eating them there, as the heathen do in the idol’s temple.

“What say I then? that the idol is any thing, or that which is offered in sacrifice to idols is any thing?” No: as he said in chapter 8, idols are nothing in the world. “But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.” The context is flee from idolatry.

“Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils”: you can’t be an idolater and serve God at the same time. “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?” as our fathers did in the wilderness, earlier in the chapter.

“All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient.” The things the heathen offer and sacrifice to idols are often clean meat. It could be unclean, but sometimes it’s clean, so it is lawful to eat. But depending on the setting it is not appropriate. In the idol’s temple the meat is fine, but where you are eating it is not expedient, not suitable. “All things edify not”: as he said earlier, charity edifieth.
“Let no man seek his own, but every man another’s wealth”: let no man be selfish, but look out for your brother who has the weak conscience. The thought continues from chapter 8.

“Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat”: the shambles are the meat markets. The meat left over in the idol’s temple was often sent off to the meat markets, a source of income for the pagan priests, and Israel would go and buy it there. Today you’ll say it’s unlawful to eat meat sacrificed to idols. Is it lawful to eat genetically modified food? That ain’t real meat, real beet, real lettuce. A strawberry this big, broccoli this big: is that real? Unless you’ve got your own land, your own farm and your own seeds, you don’t know, because they’ve got GMO seeds too. Seedless grapes and seedless watermelon are science, not God. So you’re caught between a rock and a hard place.

“Asking no question for conscience sake”: what question would you ask? Was it sacrificed to an idol? There’s no reason to ask, because idols are nothing in the world. Dig deep enough into what’s in the food and you’ll find something; that’s the point. Is there gelatin in it? Is it pork? No? Then eat it, and don’t ask no damn questions. If the meat is lawful, buy it. Obviously, if it’s wrapped up and looks weird, or you get it home and it smells funny, put it down and get rid of it for conscience sake. But if it is clearly chicken, beef, lamb or salmon as far as you know, eat it, asking no question, because you are trying your best in captivity to eat what God says to eat and drink what God says to drink.

The marketplace meat is disconnected from the idol’s temple worship. It is not the same place: it is sold for public use, like a Walmart, a ShopRite or a Costco today, so it is less offensive than eating at the actual temple. If they cut the meat, say all hail Zeus and put it on Costco’s truck, are you not going to eat the chicken because of Zeus? He ain’t a real guy in the first place. Paul permits eating meat bought in the shambles because it is no longer part of the idol feast; that is how the early believers lived in a pagan society without taking part in idolatry.

There is no contradiction between chapters 8 and 10 when you keep God’s commandments. When you are in sin and wickedness, worldly, and you hate Paul’s letters, you’ll find fault. Some of you make things complicated for no reason.

“If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go”: say they want to learn the Bible with you and invite you to their house for dinner, and you want to go. “Whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake”: whatever lawful food is set before you. Don’t ask where the meat came from, is this real chicken, real lamb, real beef, is the water tap or alkaline. It’s water. Drink the damn water.

“But if any man say unto you, This is offered in sacrifice unto idols, eat not”: this is Thanksgiving dinner, a Christmas dinner, Halloween candy, a Valentine’s Day dinner. Don’t eat it. Not because the idol is anything, not because Thanksgiving means anything or Christmas is real, but because you’ll leave a bad example: teaching against it, but eating in honour of it. You’ll offend the unbelievers. “For his sake that shewed it, and for conscience sake”: because he told you what it is. I’m sorry, I don’t celebrate that; I can’t eat that. “For the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof”: the meat on that plate is from God anyway, not from the idol it is offered in honour of.

Take Thanksgiving. If you eat it on Thanksgiving, you are destroying the people around you, because you are supposed to be an Israelite, and we don’t celebrate these days. But after Thanksgiving, after the idol worship is gone, if you have means to get food, get food; and if you don’t have the means, the food that is left has nothing to do with Thanksgiving any more, because the food is lawful. Still, for conscience sake, don’t destroy somebody weak in the spirit, because they are watching you as an Israelite.

“Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other”: by conscience Paul does not mean your own, but the conscience of the person who offers the food. “For why is my liberty judged of another man’s conscience?” You may ask among yourselves, why should it matter what he thinks? I know idols are nothing; what’s the big deal?

“For if I by grace be a partaker, why am I evil spoken of for that for which I give thanks?” If I, knowing by the grace of God that idols are nothing, eat the food he tells me is a Christmas or Thanksgiving dinner, now I look like a hypocrite: teaching against it, but eating in honour of it, and making the person think it’s okay to sacrifice to idols. So you deny the food, not because the food is bad, but because of what it is in honour of.

In the idol’s temple, don’t eat there, because you’ll cause offence to your brother. Here, don’t eat that food, because you’ll have them convinced you are eating in honour of the idol. The whole premise of both chapters, 8 and 10, is to be an example.

“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God”: whatever you do, make sure it is a good example to the glory of God. “Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles”, the northern kingdom, “nor to the church of God”: no one in the church, whether they have a strong conscience or a weak one regarding idolatry and meat sacrificed to idols. “Not seeking mine own profit”, not selfish or puffed up, “but the profit of many, that they may be saved”: winning souls by being a good example.

precepts.why:
The Corinthians were Israelites in Greece, not in Jerusalem, and our people scattered among the nations were forced to buy food from the public marketplace. “Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the Lord shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst”: serving our enemies for food, relying on them for it. The food those enemies provide is often offered to idols, or not real food at all: fake candy, fake water, fake rice, fake chicken, fake lamb, fake beef. The package says this is real cotton, this is real linen. Is it? You don’t really know. You go by faith; that’s all you can do.

“And in nakedness”: in your clothing. “And in want of all things”: whatever you desire, your enemies provide. “And he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck”: that is slavery.

“They shall not dwell in the Lord’s land; but Ephraim shall return to Egypt”: back to slavery. “And they shall eat unclean things in Assyria”: we will eat unclean things in captivity.

Dig into the ingredients deep enough and you’re going to find a problem. Potassium sorbate: what the hell is that? Keep digging if you want to, and you’ll keep finding something.

“Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the Gentiles”: the food we eat is defiled. It is not the food God commanded: we cut the animal a certain kind of way and bled the chicken out. Now we eat whatever we buy in the market.

If you can afford Whole Foods, where Esau gets the healthier food, it expires fast because it’s real food; the chicken from the hood supermarket lasts in the fridge for weeks. Not all of us can afford good food, because we are in captivity and don’t all make that kind of money, so we do what we can. Some of you negroes online trying to make Paul look bad are making yourselves look real stupid.

An Old Testament example of being an example regarding meat, and where Paul got it from, because Paul was a prophet the Lord was dealing with. “Eleazar, one of the principal scribes, an aged man”, was “constrained to open his mouth, and to eat swine’s flesh”: the Greeks wanted us to eat pork in honour of an idol. “But he, choosing rather to die gloriously, than to live stained with such an abomination, spit it forth, and came of his own accord to the torment”: I’m not eating no pork in front of these people. Just kill me.

Those in charge of that wicked feast, for their old acquaintance with him, besought him “to bring flesh of his own provision, such as was lawful for him to use, and make as if he did eat of the flesh taken from the sacrifice commanded by the king”: get your own meat that you eat according to the law, and pretend it’s pork in front of the people, so they all think you’re eating in honour of the king, “That in so doing he might be delivered from death”.

“But he began to consider discreetly”: it’s not pork, it’s clean food; if I eat it I survive, if I don’t I die. And he “willed them straightways to send him to the grave.” “For it becometh not our age, said he, in any wise to dissemble, whereby many young persons might think that Eleazar, being fourscore years old and ten, were now gone to a strange religion”: the young persons are the weak conscience, and he was ninety years old. They “through mine hypocrisy” would be deceived by him. Though he might be delivered from the punishment of men, he would not “escape the hand of the Almighty, neither alive, nor dead.”

Verse 28 is the key verse: “And leave a notable example to such as be young to die willingly and courageously for the honourable and holy laws.” He considered his people: even if I can eat food that’s lawful and pretend it’s unlawful, I still ain’t doing it. He did the exact same thing Paul said to do in 1 Corinthians 8 and 1 Corinthians 10.

sense.text: “The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.” The Lord waits for us patiently to repent and turn to him before he brings forth destruction.

“Even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you”: Peter acknowledged that wisdom was given to Paul, that the spirit of Christ was residing in Paul. That is what wisdom is.

“As also in all his epistles”: not some, not a few; all his epistles. Peter read all of Paul’s letters. “In which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest”: they twist Paul’s words to mean something else. Paul says one wife, and they say wife there means church. No, one wife means one wife. That is one of the main reasons they attack Paul: Paul gave opinions, that’s just advice. No, it’s law. Paul gives the distinction himself: staying unmarried is advice, not law, and he lets you know when it’s law and when it’s not, when it’s Christ and when it’s Moses. They wrest his letters “as they do also the other scriptures”, the Old Testament, “unto their own destruction.”

Modern scholars push the dates of the books later on purpose to remove the prophecy from them, as they say Daniel was written in the time of the Greeks, so go by the early traditional dates. 1 Corinthians was written around 54 to 55 AD, and 1 and 2 Peter shortly before Peter’s martyrdom under Nero, between about 64 and 68 AD. So if Paul wrote an erroneous letter to Israel saying worship idols, why didn’t Peter check him? Ten years, and nothing. John was alive, Andrew was not killed until after Paul wrote Corinthians and had time to check him, and Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, James, Jude, Simon and Matthias were all alive when Paul wrote Corinthians, and none of them checked him. They had five or ten years to do it, and didn’t. That would make all the remaining disciples negligent idiots who sat around and let Paul write erroneous letters. When you attack Paul you are doing yourself a disservice.

By the traditional dates Paul’s letters came first: Galatians about 48 AD, 1 Thessalonians 49 to 51, 2 Thessalonians 50 to 51, 1 Corinthians 53 to 54, 2 Corinthians 55 to 56, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon and Ephesians 57 to 62, Timothy, Titus and possibly Hebrews 63 to 65. The Gospels came afterwards: Mark 60 to 70, Matthew 65 to 85, Luke 65 to 95, John 75 to 100. So the Lord moved an idiot, a man who wrote a bunch of mistakes, to write letters that go before the disciples’ writings? Stop doing this to yourselves.

“How thou canst not bear them which are evil”: that’s us. We cannot stand it. “And thou hast tried them which say they are apostles, and are not”: those who say they are prophets and priests online, “and hast found them liars.” They lie on Paul, just as the scribes and Pharisees back then sent spies among Christ and Paul, and they flex about it the same way.

Jesus went up into the temple and taught, “And the Jews marvelled, saying, How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?” What are the letters? The letters were written by the prophets. Isaiah wrote letters, Jeremiah wrote letters; all the prophets wrote letters. And Paul wrote letters. So Paul was a prophet.

When we say we follow the law and the prophets, it ain’t just Moses and the Old Testament prophets. It’s more than that.

“Wherefore, behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes”: Christ’s own red letters. Christ sent prophets. The scribes would be Mark, who historically was Peter’s scribe and wrote for him, which is why Peter has no gospel; Luke was a scribe; Timothy was a scribe.

“And some of them ye shall kill and crucify; and some of them shall ye scourge in your synagogues, and persecute them from city to city”. Was Paul beaten in the synagogues? Yes, he was. Was Paul sent? Yes, he was. Did he persecute from city to city before he repented, and did it happen to him later on? Yes. What does that make him? A prophet.

precepts.why:
Luke the scribe explains it more. “Therefore also said the wisdom of God”: the same wisdom Peter perceived dwelt in Paul in 2 Peter. “I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute”: where Matthew says prophets, wise men and scribes, Luke says prophets and apostles. Christ sent forth prophets and apostles, and they are one and the same. “That the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation.”

So when we say we follow the law and the prophets, it ain’t just from Moses to Malachi. It’s from Moses all the way to Paul, all the way to John. That’s the law and the prophets, because Christ said, I will send prophets. Are we going to ignore the prophets Christ sent and follow only the ones who came after Moses? That’s pharisaical. We follow the apostles and prophets that Christ sent.
